entries.finding: hint 3 paraphrases the answer and gives away Q3 (the old and the new)
entries.reason: 'a clash between ways of life ... the customs and ideas each one defends' is tradition against modernity, and it also answers sibling Q3 before the student reaches it.
entries.change: Hint 3 now asks which remaining option can be supported by events across the whole play (bride-price quarrel, railway story, Sidi's final choice).

entries.finding: hint leaks Q3
entries.reason: Same words as the Codex finding; fixed by the same change.
entries.change: See the Codex entry for Q1.

entries.finding: comedy defined as always ending happily; farce described as 'little sense'
entries.reason: Check 11: a happy ending is typical of comedy, not essential. 'Wild, silly action with little sense' misdescribes farce, which rests on exaggerated, unlikely situations and physical humour. The proposed rewrites of the B and D lines were not needed: the B line is correct and the D line already says 'wild, unlikely action and slapstick'.
entries.change: Principle now says 'usually ends happily'. Hint 3 describes farce as relying on 'exaggerated, unlikely situations and physical clowning'. B and D lines unchanged.

entries.finding: teaching asserts iya-ilu and omele are not named in the play; D folded into the C line
entries.reason: The draft stated as fact what the play does and does not name, which the reviewer disputes and which cannot be checked from the item. The teaching should rest on the expected pair without denying other drums. The fourth printed option (Gangan and Omele) deserves its own line, as the draft already does for Q15.
entries.change: Hint 2 now eliminates options without the bata; hint 3 asks which partner goes with the bata. Principle scoped to 'the pair of drums this question expects'. A and C lines no longer claim the play omits those drums. Added a separate line for 'Gangan and Omele (printed run into option C)'. Codex's proposed wording that 'Iya-llu' fails only on spelling was not used, because the misprint is a typesetting slip, not a reason.

entries.finding: 'agree to it quietly' as a definition of accept
entries.reason: Check 11: acceptance need not be quiet. Alison's quiet manner is described separately and stays.
entries.change: Definition now reads 'to agree to it or go along with it, even without joy'.

entries.finding: hint 3 eliminates fool and idiot, leaving peasant
entries.reason: Calling two options 'ordinary insults for a silly person' and the answer the word that 'mocks Cliff's lack of learning' lets the student answer without recalling the scene.
entries.change: Hint 3 now asks the student to recall Jimmy's exact words when he calls Cliff ignorant over the Sunday papers.

entries.finding: hint 3 answerable by 'opposite of illusion'
entries.reason: With B and A left, 'something similar or its opposite' picks reality mechanically.
entries.change: Hint 3 now asks which pair covers both Theseus's court and the enchanted night in the wood.

entries.finding: hint 3 makes 'controlled' automatic by repeating 'by law'
entries.reason: Hint 3 named 'the kind of tenancy they hold under the rent law' against 'age' and asked which stops removal by law, which is the answer. Codex's replacement was not used as written because 'after Mr Noble's court cases' adds an unverified plot detail.
entries.change: Hint 3 now asks the student to recall the word the novel uses for these tenants and match it to an option.

entries.finding: hint 2 says Kantamanto is not an airport, which removes A, B and D at once
entries.reason: 'Kantamanto and Makola are both names of places in Accra, and neither is an airport' rules out every option containing Kantamanto, so hint 2 hands over C and hint 3 has no work left.
entries.change: Hint 2 now rules out only the option naming Makola. Hint 3 asks which pair names the main airports of Lagos and Accra.

entries.finding: 'endless, unrewarded labour', 'little reward' and 'nothing in the poem is joyful' unsupported or absolute
entries.reason: Check 11: 'nothing in the poem is joyful' is an unscoped absolute, and the reward claims go beyond what the answer needs. Lamentation stands on the poem's grief. Codex's 'fading place in memory' wording was not added, as it is not needed and cannot be checked here.
entries.change: Principle, How to tell and hint 2 now speak of the women's hardship, servitude and pain. C line now reads 'whatever moments of celebration the poem holds, its main feeling is sorrow, not excitement'.

entries.finding: 'unrhymed lines' and 'does not rhyme' false; hints test 'whether line endings rhyme at all'
entries.reason: The draft built everything on the poem having no rhyme at all, which the reviewer says is false. The defensible reading of the key is that no single rhyme scheme runs through the whole poem, with blank verse used in its loose classroom sense. Codex's specific rhyme pairs, line count and stanza count were not used, because they cannot be checked here. The teaching is right whether a few lines rhyme or none do.
entries.change: Hints 1 and 3 now test for one pattern across the whole poem; hint 2, on the sonnet, is unchanged. Solution rewritten: blank verse scoped to the loose classroom sense, 'Scattered rhymes do not make a rhyme scheme', and the C and D lines now say the pattern does not run all the way through. Exam tip now says to check the whole poem.

entries.finding: 'a didactic poem teaches a lesson openly' too absolute
entries.reason: Check 11: a didactic poem's main aim is to teach, usually but not always by stating the lesson directly, and satire can overlap with it. One qualifier fixes this.
entries.change: Hint 1 now says 'set out a lesson for the reader'. Hint 3 now says 'a poem whose main aim is to teach'. B line now says 'usually by stating its lesson directly' and admits that the poem carries a warning.

entries.finding: 'Metaphor is a single comparison' is a false absolute
entries.reason: A metaphor can be extended, and allegory is often called an extended metaphor.
entries.change: Hint 2 now says metaphor 'names a comparison'. A line now says the poem does compare, but when a whole story stands for something else the more exact name is allegory.

entries.finding: ending overstated as hope 'that Africa will be free' and a 'struggle for freedom'
entries.reason: The closing affirms that Africa and its people live on and endure, not a predicted freedom. Optimistic still stands on that. Codex's direct quotations were not added, because they cannot be checked here.
entries.change: Hint 3, principle and How to tell now describe the close as affirming that Africa and its people are still alive and will endure.

entries.finding: hint 3 defines tone, which identifies D
entries.reason: 'Simply the speaker's feeling towards the creatures' is the definition of tone, so the student can pick D without thinking.
entries.change: Hint 3 now asks which of setting and attitude can stand for an idea beyond itself.

entries.finding: 'ends unsure whether ... Birth or Death' misreports the ending
entries.reason: The speaker asks the question, then says the Birth was certain and felt like the death of his old life.
entries.change: How to tell now says he asks the question and finds that the Birth felt like a hard death of his old life.

entries.finding: 'not replaced by factories' is a false test for industrialization
entries.reason: Industry can harm nature without factories replacing the trees, and the poem does not say why the trees were felled.
entries.change: A line now says the poem does not name industry as the cause; its direct focus is the destruction of the trees and the landscape.

entries.finding: 'ends with a joke' stated as universal
entries.reason: Check 11: a punchline is typical of a limerick, not a rule.
entries.change: How to tell now says 'usually ends with a funny twist'.

entries.finding: hint 2 lists 'hills, rivers, flowers and birds', which points to Nature; D line says ordinary people are not what Romanticism celebrated
entries.reason: Hint 2 described nature in all but name, so it gave the answer. Ordinary rural people were a real Romantic concern, as with Wordsworth's 'common life'.
entries.change: Hint 2 now rules out life and people as subjects of every period. Hint 3 now narrows to beauty against nature without describing either. D line now admits Wordsworth wrote about ordinary people and says 'people' is too broad. Hint 1 now says 'is often remembered' (check 11). Codex's A-line rewrite was not needed: the existing A line is already accurate.

entries.finding: hint 3 gives away 'sudden'; 'middle of the action' too narrow; definition and Oedipus summary compressed
entries.reason: 'A single turning moment ... not a long process' maps directly onto sudden against gradual. A reversal need not fall in the middle. The intended-result wording is Aristotle's example, not his whole definition. The messenger reveals the adoption, which starts the discovery, not the whole truth at once.
entries.change: Hint 2 now says 'a turn in the action'. Hint 3 asks the student to test each option against the direction and speed of a tragic hero's change of luck. Principle now says the action 'swings round to its opposite, often when a deed meant to bring one result brings the opposite'. How to tell now says the messenger reveals the adoption and sets off the discovery.

entries.finding: 'not about a real tree and a real building' false either-or; 'nothing about them is exaggerated' absolute
entries.reason: Check 11: the objects are real in the poem and symbolic too, and 'a huge, senseless cathedral of doom' is strong language. Hint 2 carried the same absolute ('they are not exaggerated'), so it was scoped out as well.
entries.change: The How to tell sentence now says they are real objects that also stand for the change. The C line now says the cathedral is described in strong words but the pair mainly work as symbols. Removed 'and they are not exaggerated' from hint 2.

entries.finding: sibling sweep of all passage groups (s01 to s10)
entries.reason: Only the Q1 hint 3 leak into Q3 was found. Solutions that name sibling facts, such as Q33's C line naming the denouement before Q40, are allowed by the standard.
entries.change: None beyond Q1.

entries.finding: hint 2 and solution line C define 'solemnizing' only as performing a ceremony and claim it cannot name a tone
entries.reason: Dictionaries also give 'to make solemn or grave', so the claim that the word is not a tone a poem ends on is false. The elimination must rest on the poem's hopeful ending.
entries.change: Hint 2 now says 'solemnizing' would mean a grave, formal ending and groups it with the sad options, without saying the close is hopeful (Codex's wording 'closing lines are hopeful' would hand over the answer in hint 2). Hint 3 reworded to match, since C is no longer eliminated outright. Solution line C now rests on the hopeful close.

entries.finding: sibling leak check across Q22 to Q26 (s07)
entries.reason: Q26's hints mention only Neto's poem and its ending; nothing answers Q22 to Q25.

entries.finding: unscoped absolutes
entries.reason: After the fix no absolute remains; 'Many protest poems' is already hedged.
